client: I've been having a really hard time since my grandmother passed away last month. I just can't seem to focus at work — I'll sit down to do something and then completely zone out, sometimes for like an hour, and I don't even realize it. I'm not sure talking about it is actually going to help, but I figured I should at least try something because it's starting to affect my job.
therapist: Thank you for taking that step and showing up today, even with the uncertainty about whether it will help — that takes real courage, especially when you're carrying something this heavy. Losing your grandmother and then trying to hold everything together at work sounds genuinely exhausting, and the zoning out you're describing is actually a very common way grief shows up in our minds and bodies, not a sign that something is wrong with you. I'd love to gently explore together what's happening in those moments when your mind drifts — there may be more going on beneath the surface that, once we understand it, can start to ease some of that weight.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I guess it's a little reassuring to hear that the zoning out isn't just me being lazy or broken, because honestly that's kind of what I've been telling myself. When I drift off, I think I'm usually remembering things about her — like specific moments, her voice, stuff like that — and then I feel this wave of guilt because I'm supposed to be working and instead I'm just... lost in it. I don't really know what understanding it better would change, though, because she's still gone no matter what.
therapist: The way you're speaking — softly, almost like you're holding something fragile — tells me this grief is sitting very deep right now, and I want to gently push back on that guilt: your mind drifting to her voice and those memories isn't a failure, it's love that doesn't have anywhere to go yet. You're absolutely right that understanding it won't bring her back, and I won't pretend otherwise — but what it *can* change is whether you spend this time grieving her *and* punishing yourself, versus just grieving her. That self-critical story you've been telling yourself — "lazy, broken" — is an extra weight on top of an already unbearable one, and you don't have to carry both.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: That framing — "love that doesn't have anywhere to go" — actually hit me harder than I expected, and I had to take a second there. But I'm not sure I know how to just stop being hard on myself about it, because the guilt feels almost automatic, like it kicks in before I even have a chance to think. It's like my brain is wired to go straight to "you're failing" before I can catch it.
therapist: The way you're speaking — quickly, with a kind of tension in your voice — makes me think that even describing this pattern is activating it a little right now, and that actually makes complete sense. You've named something really important though: that "you're failing" thought feels automatic because it's been practiced so many times it's become a reflex, not a truth — and in CBT we call these automatic thoughts, and the good news is that reflexes *can* be interrupted, not by forcing yourself to stop feeling guilty, but by learning to notice it just a half-second sooner each time. That pause you took when something landed differently just now? That *is* the catching — it's already starting.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: Okay, I can see what you're saying about noticing it sooner, but I'm a little skeptical that a half-second pause is really going to do much when I'm in the middle of a workday and the guilt just crashes over me. It feels like trying to catch a wave with your hands — like, what am I actually supposed to do in that moment even if I do notice it? I don't want to just sit there at my desk feeling the guilt and then still not be able to work.
therapist: Your skepticism is completely fair, and I'd rather work with something real than sell you a technique that sounds nice but doesn't hold up when the wave actually hits. So here's something concrete: when you notice that guilt crash in, the goal isn't to feel it and push through — it's to briefly name it out loud or in your head, something like "there's that guilt again," which actually interrupts the automatic loop just enough to give you a tiny foothold. It sounds almost too simple, but that small act of naming shifts you from being *inside* the wave to being someone who's *watching* it, and from there, getting back to work becomes possible rather than impossible.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: I mean, I can try that, but I'm a little worried that saying "there's that guilt again" is just going to make me more aware of it and then I'll spiral into thinking about her even more, which is the opposite of what I need at work. I guess what I'm not sure about is whether I'm actually supposed to let myself feel it for a second or just kind of acknowledge it and immediately redirect — because those feel like really different things to me.
therapist: The way you're asking this — softly but quickly, like your mind is working hard to find solid ground — tells me this distinction really matters to you, and it's actually a really sharp question. The honest answer is it's neither pure feeling nor pure redirecting — it's a brief acknowledgment, like touching the guilt for just a second to say "I see you" without inviting it to stay for the whole meeting, and then gently turning your attention back. The fear that noticing will open a floodgate makes complete sense, but what usually causes the spiral isn't the noticing — it's the *fighting* it or the guilt *about* the guilt that keeps pulling you back under.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: The "guilt about the guilt" thing actually makes a lot of sense to me, because I think that's exactly what happens — I feel bad about drifting, and then I feel bad about feeling bad, and suddenly I've lost twenty minutes just cycling through that. I'm willing to try the "I see you" thing, but I guess my worry is that at work there's no privacy, I'm in an open office, and it already feels embarrassing that I'm not functioning the way I normally do. I don't want my coworkers to notice that something's off with me on top of everything else.
therapist: The way you're speaking — softly but quickly, like you're trying to get through something that feels a little exposed — makes me think the vulnerability of being seen struggling might actually be harder than the grief itself right now. The good news is that "I see you" never has to be spoken out loud — it's entirely internal, just a quiet flicker of recognition that happens in your own mind while you look perfectly normal to everyone around you. And it's worth gently noticing that the story "my coworkers can see I'm not functioning" is another one of those automatic thoughts — most people are far more focused on their own work than on monitoring you, even when it feels absolutely certain that they're not.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: That's actually a relief to hear that it stays internal, because I think I'd been imagining I'd have to do something visible or weird at my desk. But I'm not totally convinced about the coworker thing — like, my manager actually did ask me last week if I was okay, which felt like confirmation that people are noticing, not just something I'm making up. So that automatic thought might not be entirely wrong in my case.
therapist: You're right to push back on that, and it's actually good critical thinking — your manager asking if you're okay is real evidence, and I don't want to dismiss it. But there's an important distinction worth sitting with: your manager noticing that you seem to be going through something hard is very different from them seeing you as failing or broken — in fact, someone checking in on you is more likely concern than judgment. The story to examine isn't "no one notices anything," but rather "what does it mean if they do notice, and is that meaning as catastrophic as it feels right now?"
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I hadn't really thought about it that way — that my manager checking in might just be concern rather than her keeping tabs on my performance. But I think what scares me is that if I let myself believe it's just concern, and then it turns out my job is actually at risk, I'll have let my guard down for nothing and that'll feel even worse. It's like the worry is almost protecting me from a bigger disappointment.
therapist: The quietness in your voice right now, almost like you're saying something you haven't quite let yourself say out loud before, makes me think you just named something really important — that the worry feels like armor, not just a burden. What you're describing is actually a very human and understandable strategy: if I stay braced for the worst, at least the fall won't surprise me. But it's worth gently asking — is the constant bracing actually protecting you, or is it costing you something every single day while the thing you're afraid of may never even happen?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, very quiet, moderate-paced speech

client: Honestly, when you put it that way, I can feel that the bracing is exhausting — like I've been tensed up for a month straight and I haven't even noticed how much energy that's taking. But I don't really know how to just... stop doing it, because it feels like if I relax even a little, I'm being naive or setting myself up. I think part of me believes that worrying hard enough about something is the same as being prepared for it, even though I know logically that's not really true.
therapist: The way you're speaking — soft but quick, like something is finally surfacing after being held down for a long time — tells me that recognizing this exhaustion is both a relief and a little frightening. You've actually just identified a core belief worth examining: that worry equals preparation, and relaxing equals naivety — but preparation is something you *do*, while worry is something that *happens to you*, and one actually gets you ready while the other just keeps you depleted. The goal isn't to stop caring about your job or drop your guard entirely — it's to trade that constant low-grade bracing for something more intentional, so you're not spending a month's worth of energy defending against something that may never come.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: The distinction between worry and preparation is actually sticking with me, because I think I've been confusing them for so long that they feel like the same thing. But I'm not sure what "more intentional" actually looks like in practice — like, what would I do instead of the constant bracing that would still make me feel like I'm taking my situation seriously? I don't want to just replace one thing with nothing and feel like I'm floating.
therapist: The speed and pitch in your voice right now tells me this question feels urgent — like you can see the problem clearly but need something solid to hold onto before you can let the old pattern go, and that makes complete sense. Intentional preparation, in practice, might look like one specific action — checking in briefly with your manager, or identifying one concrete thing you'd do *if* your job were actually at risk — so that your mind has real evidence that you're handling it, rather than just bracing endlessly against a vague threat. Once you've done that one thing, when the worry creeps back you can remind yourself: "I've already prepared — this is just the worry talking, not useful information."
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech
